sourceVariantTitle: Why Did That Message Sound Rude?
scoreRule: One point per correct answer; ten points maximum. Provisional local result only.
description: Original English B2 independent Reading draft with ten inference and transfer questions; requires later pedagogical review.

tabs.title: Reading Between the Lines
tabs.description: Understand the role of missing context and expectations.

tabs.title: Evaluating the Examples
tabs.description: Explain why misunderstandings happen and how they develop.

tabs.title: Clearer Communication
tabs.description: Choose practical responses in new situations.

questions.q: Why can 'OK.' seem unfriendly even when the sender is not upset?
choices: The full stop always indicates anger in English.
The sender is required to add an emoji to every text.
The reader lacks the voice, expression and situation that would clarify the reply.
A one-word reply can only be written in a hurry.
questions.explanation: The article explains that missing social context can change the interpretation of text, and suggests clarification rather than assumptions.

questions.q: Why might an older relative and a younger friend understand the same punctuation differently?
choices: Older relatives do not understand written grammar.
They may follow different expectations about how a short text should look.
Young people are unable to read a complete sentence.
They are necessarily using different messaging applications.
questions.explanation: The article explains that missing social context can change the interpretation of text, and suggests clarification rather than assumptions.

questions.q: What does the comparison between a fast and slow reply illustrate?
choices: A slow response is more truthful than a quick one.
Teachers and employers usually respond faster than friends.
The sender's intentions change whenever the message is delayed.
Timing can influence the reader's interpretation even when the words stay the same.
questions.explanation: The article explains that missing social context can change the interpretation of text, and suggests clarification rather than assumptions.

questions.q: Why does Marek's later question surprise Dana?
choices: She had treated his agreement as disapproval and changed her plans.
She had never told Marek about the farewell present.
Marek had ordered a different photo book without telling anyone.
Their teacher had already received the planned gift.
questions.explanation: The article explains that missing social context can change the interpretation of text, and suggests clarification rather than assumptions.

questions.q: What does the writer achieve by stating that nobody was rude in the example?
choices: The two students are shown to have identical views about the book.
Their delay is presented as a direct result of poor school rules.
The problem is shown as a mistaken interpretation rather than deliberate hostility.
The group's original plan is described as impossible to complete.
questions.explanation: The article explains that missing social context can change the interpretation of text, and suggests clarification rather than assumptions.

questions.q: Why does the writer reject making every message long and formal?
choices: That change could feel unnatural and introduce new misunderstandings.
Long messages cannot be sent in group chats.
Formal writing always prevents friendly communication.
Students should avoid using full sentences altogether.
questions.explanation: The article explains that missing social context can change the interpretation of text, and suggests clarification rather than assumptions.

questions.q: What is the likely benefit of agreeing that a thumbs-up means 'seen, will answer later'?
choices: The group can make decisions without ever discussing them.
Members have a shared explanation for a signal that might otherwise be unclear.
People no longer need to answer important questions.
The signal prevents anyone from changing their mind.

questions.q: Your friend writes an unexpectedly short response about an upsetting event. What first step follows the article's advice?
choices: Stop responding for several days to show that you are hurt.
Assume the person is rejecting your friendship.
Send the message to classmates and ask them to interpret it.
Ask whether you have understood the intended meaning before drawing conclusions.
questions.explanation: The article explains that missing social context can change the interpretation of text, and suggests clarification rather than assumptions.

questions.q: A group must agree on tomorrow's event, but one student replies 'fine'. Which follow-up is most useful?
choices: Avoid making a decision until the student adds an emoji.
Confirm explicitly that the student agrees with the proposed plan.
Choose a different event without asking anyone.
Interpret the shortest message as the strongest opposition.
questions.explanation: The article explains that missing social context can change the interpretation of text, and suggests clarification rather than assumptions.

questions.q: A disagreement keeps becoming more emotional through typed messages. Which response most closely fits the conclusion?
choices: Add more punctuation to each reply until the other person agrees.
Continue texting because changing channels would appear old-fashioned.
Wait several days before asking whether anything is wrong.
Suggest a call or face-to-face discussion to restore missing context.
questions.explanation: The article explains that missing social context can change the interpretation of text, and suggests clarification rather than assumptions.
